title: food as practice
hook: a young man asks his father what Brahman is, and the first answer he finds is food

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the seasons: Charaka's year, every season answered with its opposite, ending in swan water and moonlight.

A son goes to his father with one request. Teach me Brahman, he says: the ultimate reality, the ground of everything. His name is Bhrigu. His father is Varuna. And Varuna doesn't lecture. He gives a riddle and sends him away to work it out. Bhrigu goes off, sits with it, practices, and comes back with an answer that might seem almost too ordinary for the question. He says: food. A run of days on food as practice starts with that answer.
screen: `TEACH ME BRAHMAN.` → `A RIDDLE, NOT A LECTURE.` → `THE FIRST ANSWER: FOOD.`

segments.voice: The story is in the Taittiriya Upanishad. Varuna's riddle, paraphrased: that from which beings are born, by which, once born, they live, and into which they return, seek to know that. That is Brahman. And one instruction: seek it through tapas, disciplined, inward effort. So Bhrigu does, and he comes to see, the text says, that food is Brahman. From food beings are born. By food they live. Into food they return. It fits every line of the riddle. Now the twist. Varuna doesn't say, well done, you're finished. He gives the same instruction again, seek it through tapas, and sends him out once more. Step by step Bhrigu goes deeper: to breath, to mind, to understanding, and at last to bliss. Three things. First, food isn't thrown away when he goes deeper. It's the first floor of the house, and the house stands on it. Second, the Upanishad draws vows out of it. Do not speak ill of food. Do not despise food. Make much food. Not diet rules but a stance: food handled with respect, because it was the first thing Bhrigu found holy. Third, the Ayurvedic texts arrive somewhere close from another direction. Charaka treats food as what sustains the life of living beings, the ground health is built on, which is why these days give food a whole week. So food as practice doesn't start with a rule about what to eat. It starts with seeing what food is.
screen: `BHRIGU ASKS HIS FATHER` · `FOOD IS BRAHMAN` · `SEARCH AGAIN, AND GO DEEPER` · `DO NOT SPEAK ILL OF FOOD`

segments.voice: Bring to mind the last thing you ate, then follow it backward: the hands that served it, the kitchen, the shop, the truck, the field or the sea, the rain and the sun that ripened it. Go slowly, as far back as you can, and let it become a long line of things you didn't make. If you pray, give thanks for one link in that line.
Food as practice. In the Taittiriya Upanishad, food is the first thing Bhrigu recognizes as Brahman, and the vow that follows: do not speak ill of food. Today's word.
Your line: food as practice. Bhrigu's first answer was food, and he never threw it away. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: In Hindu homes that keep these customs, food is offered before it is eaten, and complaining about food or wasting it is avoided, a stance the Taittiriya Upanishad puts as a vow not to speak ill of food.

fork.setup: you're Varuna. your son comes back from his search and says, food is Brahman. what do you do?
options: send him out to search again, through tapas.
tell him food has nothing to do with Brahman.
fork.reveal: Varuna repeats the instruction to seek through tapas, and Bhrigu goes deeper, to breath, mind, understanding and bliss. Food isn't wrong; it's the first floor.

original.note: Sanskrit: anna, food. In the Taittiriya Upanishad, Bhrigu first comes to see that food is Brahman.

chat.says: Wait, an Upanishad says food is Brahman? Isn't Brahman way beyond lunch?
options: Food was Bhrigu's first answer; his father sent him deeper, but food stays the first floor.
Food was Bhrigu's only answer, so the Upanishad says nothing lies deeper than food.
Food was a wrong answer, so his father told him to give up eating and go deeper.
chat.meaning: In the Taittiriya, Bhrigu first finds food is Brahman, then goes deeper to breath, mind, understanding and bliss; food stays the ground: do not speak ill of food.

Bhrigu.meaning: the son who asks his father to teach him Brahman

notes: First of seven food-as-practice days (1307–1313). This writer's plan: 1307 food is Brahman, 1308 measure, 1309 the way of eating, 1310 the Gita's three kinds of food, 1311 sharing food. 1312–1313 belong to another writer.

Taittiriya 3.1–3.10: confirm the paraphrase of Varuna's riddle, that Varuna repeats it each time, and the sequence food, breath, mind, understanding, bliss. Max Müller's 1884 translation exists (SBE 15) but wording was not quoted because it could not be verified word for word.
Taittiriya 3.7–3.9 vows (annam na nindyat, annam na parichaksita, annam bahu kurvita): confirm verse numbers.
Charaka Sutrasthana 27: confirm a statement that food sustains the life of living beings (often cited near the chapter's end).
howItsDone generalizes about Hindu homes that keep these customs (offering food first, not wasting or complaining); confirm wording.
